1.title: Altenberg de Bergheim: The Model of Blending on Red Marl
1.html:
Altenberg de Bergheim (Bergheim, 35.06 ha) lies on the Ribeauvillé fault zone, with red marl-limestone that is stony and rich in fossils. The blending rules here use an "either/or" structure:

  • Option 1: a pure single-variety wine of Riesling, Pinot Gris or Gewurztraminer
  • Option 2 (blend): Riesling 50–70%, Pinot Gris 10–25%, Gewurztraminer 10–25%, with the remaining Pinot Blanc, Pinot Noir, Muscat Ottonel, Muscat à petit grain and Chasselas together under 10% (only those already planted before 26 March 2005)

In the blended version the grapes are pressed together (pressés ensemble) — unlike the practice of some estates of "vinifying separately and then blending", this is closer to a traditional field blend, and the key source of this wine's distinctive flavour.
2.title: Kaefferkopf: Foresight Ahead of the AOC Concept
2.html:
Kaefferkopf (Ammerschwihr, 71.65 ha), with a complex geology mixing granite, oolitic limestone and sandstone, was already under legal protection in 1932 — long before the concept of the "appellation" (Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée) was formally born — making it one of the plots with the oldest reputation in the Alsace wine world.

Blending rules:

  • May be made as a pure single variety of Riesling, Pinot Gris or Gewurztraminer (with the variety name on the label)
  • Or by blend proportions: Gewurztraminer 60–80%, Riesling 10–40%, Pinot Gris at most 30%

Blending is the signature feature of the Kaefferkopf Grand Cru, combining elegance with powerful, intense aromas — when it officially became the 51st Grand Cru in 2007, it was the only site that had expressly allowed blending since its creation.
3.title: The Two Blended Grand Crus Compared by Proportion
3.items.0.desc: Riesling 50-70% + Pinot Gris 10-25% + Gewurztraminer 10-25%, with Riesling as the dominant backbone
3.items.1.desc: Gewurztraminer 60-80% + Riesling 10-40% + Pinot Gris ≤30%, with Gewurztraminer as the dominant backbone
4.question: What special significance does the Kaefferkopf site have in the history of Alsace wine regulation?
4.options.0: It was the first Grand Cru delimited (1975)
4.options.1: It was already under legal protection in 1932, long before the concept of the "appellation" (AOC) was formally born
4.options.2: It is the only blended Grand Cru in Bas-Rhin
4.options.3: It is the smallest blended Grand Cru
4.explanation: Kaefferkopf was already under legal protection in 1932, a date long before the concept of the "appellation" (Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée) was formally born, showing that the site's outstanding reputation was recognised before the regulatory system took shape — which is also the historical root of its becoming in 2007 the 51st Grand Cru and the only one that had expressly allowed blending since its creation.
5.message: The two blended Grand Crus complete!
5.keyPoints.0: Altenberg de Bergheim: Riesling 50-70% + Pinot Gris 10-25% + Gewurztraminer 10-25%, pressed and vinified together
5.keyPoints.1: Kaefferkopf: Gewurztraminer 60-80% + Riesling 10-40% + Pinot Gris ≤30%, under legal protection as early as 1932
5.keyPoints.2: Both may choose a pure single variety or a blend by proportion, blending being the signature feature of each
5.keyPoints.3: Only these two of the 51 Grand Crus allow blending, showing the art of Alsace blending at the highest classification level
